designers: By Hannah Rose Dalton & Steven Raj Bhaskaran
reviewHtml:
“This one is for the 99%,” said Steven Raj Bhaskaran. “It’s taking the source of power from last season and giving it to the people that we want to empower.” Last season was staged in a Parisian former stock exchange and titled The 1%: it contained plenty of satirical swipes at the have-yachts, VVIC, HNWI elite that much of luxury fashion dedicates itself to chasing. This season twisted that formula inside out to transport us from plutocracy to pluralism.

Every one of the 99 models was a person of color. In a considerable feat of production—and, according to the designers, definitely a first—the show was staged beneath the Monument à la République, on a square synonymous with popular demonstration in Paris. Bhaskaran and Hannah Rose Dalton were using their fashion platform as a podium for a republican agenda: the redistribution of representation. As a way of inserting social activism into the spectacle of luxury fashion, tonight’s show was an effective Trojan horse.

Although they were required to do so for legal and safety reasons, the designers were not blind to the irony of fencing off such a sacred populist site for a fashion show designed to espouse inclusion: hence some members of the public were invited inside the barricade of privilege. All of that fashion audience—plus the many rubberneckers enjoying the view from the first-floor dining area of Five Guys across the road—had plenty of time to contemplate the monument itself. Marianne stands almost 10 meters high, personifying the French Republic, while Liberty, Equality and Fraternity are embodied in the figures beneath her. Eventually they were joined by Rihanna: we could begin.

The images that will define this show were of the final two looks (94 and 95 here) in which two young Black models carried Sarah Sitkin’s hyper-realistic statues of well-fed old white men wearing dollar-bill blindfolds. Their symbolism also served to bookend the opening looks, in which models carried swaddled infants. Between those two moments, the designers split this 35-minute show into three distinct acts.

The first was autobiographical, concluding at look 40 with a tableau of Bhaskaran, his mother Grace, his sister Shandeal and his niece Vihannna. Its religious vocabulary also came directly from his upbringing: Dalton noted that he grew up across Hindu, Christian, Mormon and Muslim environments. Bhaskaran said the covered male heads earlier in the line-up were about “veiling the male identity,” reversing a convention more usually imposed on women. He said that, in his experience, patriarchal hypermasculinity could itself function as a kind of veil, obscuring men’s “true selves.” The cross-decorated kurtas and tailoring also drew on humbler fabrics from his childhood: Bhaskaran recalled the linen skirts his mother wore around their apartment building. Sprinkled among these specifically personal references was plenty of the distressed tailoring, outerwear and eveningwear that forms one pillar of the Matières Fécales offer.

Act II was unenlighteningly illuminated: a strobed assault of flicker vertigo, muddied further by belches of look-obscuring dry ice. Despite this it was also a stirringly dynamic portrayal of the diversity of Paris. Bhaskaran called this the “protest section,” rooted partly in the punk and metal scenes through which he “found my people” after leaving home in Montreal. Leather punkery, balaclavas, body augmentations and Marianne-starring death-metal T-shirts were populated by characters he saw as defying the stereotypes attached both to their cultures and to alternative subculture itself. “This is what France looks like today,” he said. This was also the section that had the crowd whooping loudest: for Bbyafricka in denim, thigh-high Louboutin flip-flop slingbacks, facial spikes and wickedly red nails; and for a model wrapped in the French tricolore printed with the word RESIST.

Look 77’s tulle-trained gown was modeled by Monique-Antoine Orosemane, aka Mounia, the Martinican model and Yves Saint Laurent muse whose 1978 breakthrough made her one of the defining Black figures of Paris haute couture. Much of this final act was dedicated to further widening the lens of couture practice. Sari textiles made in Varanasi were reworked into 1950s couture volumes, including one silhouette built over 300 meters of tulle. Handwoven cotton from Burkina Faso was pushed into corseted eveningwear. Connecting the exclusive world of Parisian couture with the crafts and traditions of the so-called Global South felt as much pragmatic as provocative.

This Matières Fécales show was made of many parts, some of which seemed drawn from sources including Alexander McQueen, Rick Owens (who was in the audience) and Vetements. But it was also more than the sum of those parts. “I think our mission is to make it soulful,” Bhaskaran said, “and hopefully present the humanity behind fashion that is sometimes lost in these hyper-perfect products and hyper-perfect shows. Everyone is chasing belonging: the difference between the 1% and the 99% is opportunity.” Modern France is built on the promise of liberté, égalité, fraternité. Tonight Matières Fécales added visibilité.
